Some of us have a lot of experience recording, all the way up to professional studio work. Others have none, and don't know where to even begin! That being the case, let's dive in and learn stuff!

Me: I'm great on the tracking side. I know the gear, up to mid level professional studio gear. I have a good understanding of sources (mic, direct, etc), mic placement, etc. I know how to get a good capture of most things. I'm a bit spotty on drums, but good enough to make a solid recording. I've been taking classes and working on mixing skills, and don't even ask me about mastering.

So, where are you, and where do you want to be?

I am happy with what I am currently able to do. I have worked on quite a few records released on independent labels (some larger than others) and I've worked with some great people who have shown me all sorts of tips and tricks and even some ethos.

Where do I want to be? If it weren't for the brutal hours, I'd love to be engineering more original recordings! What I'll do right now is share a bit of what I've learned.

1 above all is performance. Capture a great player or a set of balanced players in a good sounding room with a mic/stereo recorder and it will work.

2 I just mentioned: Good sounding room. Dry is useful. It is way easier to add air & space than to take it away.

3 The more complex your mic set-up, the more important your mic selections and pre's are. Many cheap pre's sound decent until you 'stack' 16-24 tracks of them on top of one another. Now the deficiencies and noise are multiplied to a level where it negatively effects the whole recording.

4 Ducking. You have to duck the bass guitar when the kick hits. You have to duck the electric guitars when the vocals hit. And then start judiciously ducking everything.

5 (Maybe this should be #1.) Stav's book. Buy this now. http://mixingwithyourmind.com
Can't stress the importance of performance. Garbage in, garbage out.
Here is a good place to begin. The Wikipedia article is a surprisingly decent start.
Interesting. Thanks. I'm not sure my tascam has the capability to do that

You use an all in one recorder? Do you use separate mics or any outboard? What's the model?

Either way, during mix down, you can manually do much ducking. It's a good idea to keep in mind, instead of thinking:

"I can't hear the vocals! Need to turn them up!"
Your mind can more effectively think:
"I can't hear the vocals! Need to turn the guitars down!"

All this being said, if there is no "mix" process involved in your recordings, then head back to step 1, performance, and convince your players they must do their own ducking.

I've gone to a pretty well known school for audio recording but a career in meda production was not in my fate. I'd say I've got a good understanding of what to do and a bunch of books on how to do it. Currently learning EE while working as a rework tech, my goal is to get into the engineering/production of equipment for studio and live application.

As far as things to know I think heygeorge covered all of the key points. Some things I think are worth mentioning:

  1. Record and mix at the highest bit depth and sample rate within reason. Tipically my projects are 48k 24bit but I work in digital space a lot so its not a huge issue for me but if you are doing drums it helps keep cymballs sounding rich.

  2. Fade ALL reigons and stems before bouncing. Millisecond fades at the beginningand end of punch in reigons and at the beginning and end of the song prevent unwanted pops in the mastering phase.

  3. Always do real time bounces. Less chance of artifacts and you can monitor the bounce as it happens.

  4. DO NOT RECORD TO YOUR SYSTRM DRIVE. Certan DAWs do not look before writing and oops there goes the system32 file.

  5. Understanding how to properly use time based effects and AUX channels makes for an easier time when dealing with lots of layers.

  6. Bigger is not always better when it comes to reference monitors. I like those yamaha 6" ones. KRKs color the sound too much.

  7. Don't mix exclusivly in headphones. You will miss phase problems.

  8. Don't blow your wad on the DAW. Think like an engineer and get what you need.

  9. Practice practice practice practice... you get the picture.

The MOTU is a great interface, and most importantly is complete. MOTU has always been known for a great product. The Apollo doesn't actually come with the inputs, just the capacity to connect them via a DB25 or ethernet connection. The most important thing for you, since you're running Linux, is to make sure that drivers are available. At that price range, you could also look at the Focusrite Clarett 18i20 for your first 8 inputs paired with a Focusrite Clarett OctoPre for the next 8. I like the Clarett due to some low-latency features introduced with that product, as well as the AIR feature, which is great for drums. Here is a video that compares the Scarlett to the Clarett and demonstrates the AIR feature. Providing there are Linux drivers, both the MOTU and the Focusrite Clarett products will put you in around $1600~ for good a quality interface with 16 inputs. With the Focusrite, you have the ability to start with 8 and stack on another 8 with the OctoPre at your convenience. I also want to note that there are 3 levels of OctoPre, the highest of which comes with outboard compressors if you want that.

The MOTU is standards compliant and, from what I'm seeing, should be just fine with Linux. (Worst case, I can install a Windows VM and use that. I'm not one of the Linux zealots - I just use it 'cause it works for me. I don't actually hate Microsoft or proprietary software.)
